units.translation: O of one exclaiming with an imperative
O of one addressing with the vocative of a single noun, either substantive or adjective
O of one addressing with a substantive and an adjective, and in such a way that for metrical necessity the adjective either precedes or follows
and with the adjective placed after the noun (on which see Hermann, Opuscula 4 p. 368)
O of one addressing with a participle or adjective
O placed before two or more addresses

That the vocative is the article ὁ was the opinion of many grammarians, recorded by Apollonius in On Syntax p. 29, 25; 51, 28; 53, 21; 54, 27. He himself rejects it at p. 69, 26, because even ὦ οὗτος [O you there] is said, to which pronoun the article is not prefixed. Herodian also rejected it, from whom Arcadius p. 100, 17: τὸ ὦ ψιλοῦται · οὐ γὰρ ἄρθρον, ἀλλ᾽ ἐπίρρημα κλητικόν [the word ὦ has a smooth breathing; for it is not an article, but a vocative adverb]. Those grammarians are refuted at greater length by the scholia on Dionysius Thrax in Bekker's Anecdota p. 903 and by Helladius in Photius' Bibliotheca p. 530, 14-31, rightly calling ὦ a vocative adverb. Hesychius follows the other opinion: ὦ, ἄρθρον κλητικῆς πτώσεως, οἷον ὦ ἄνθρωπε [O, article of the vocative case, as in O man]. It is generally joined with the vocative, but often also with the nominative of nouns, adjectives, participles, and in such a way that it is either of one exclaiming or of one addressing, yet in not a few places the situation is such that it makes no difference whether ὦ is thought to be of one exclaiming, with no regard to a person, or of one addressing a certain person, whether present or absent.

Placed after the imperative. For thus Seidler corrected for ἐπολολυξάτω [let him cry aloud], and likewise at Ag. 1118 Meineke restored κατολολύξατ᾽ ὦ θύματος λευσίμου [raise a cry, O you, for the victim to be stoned] for κατολολυξάτω [let him cry aloud], Philologus vol. 19 p. 207.
where ὦ or w has been added from the copies.
where I wrote "Απoλλον [Apollo] from the copies, as it is read at 1080 and 1085, although the crasis ὤπολλον [O Apollo] is mentioned in Etymologicum Magnum p. 514, 30.
